Lab 8.5: Infer Geologic History from a New Mexico Outcrop

Work the lab one question at a time, then use the practice tab to build the same skills on new problems. Your instructor collects the lab manual worksheet; this page is for guided practice and feedback.

Figure A8.5.1 from your lab manual: an outcrop in a surface coal mine in northern New Mexico. The scale bar at lower left runs 0 to 2 m.

Start here

Read the outcrop

This outcrop has four kinds of evidence. Compare the photo with the drawing before you answer any questions.

  1. Layers. Sandstone at the bottom, shale above it, then a basalt sill, on both sides of a fault zone. In the drawing, sedimentary rock that once covered the sill is shown on the right.
  2. Fossils. Fagopsis leaf fossils are present in the shale and sandstone. Leaf fossils like these are not index fossils for a single moment, but their time range is on Figure 8.13 in your lab manual.
  3. Zircon crystals inside the basalt can be dated with U-235 → Pb-207 decay (Figure 8.14).
  4. A fault. The layers on the right are offset from the same layers on the left.
On your lab page · page 227 and 228Your answers go on the lab page, not here. 8.5A questions 1 to 3 are on page 227. 8.5B (numbered list) and 8.5C are on page 228. This site checks your thinking first, so you know what to write.

The basalt is interpreted as a sill: magma that squeezed between existing layers and cooled in place. Keep that in mind when you decide what is older and what is younger.

8.5A · Question 2

Numerical age of the sill

Zircon crystals in the sill have 98.9% U-235 remaining and 1.10% Pb-207. The half-life of U-235 is 703.8 million years. The crystals probably formed when the sill cooled, so their age is also the age of the sill.

On your lab page · page 227, 8.5A question 2Write the numerical age of the sill under question 2 and show how you calculated it: the half-lives elapsed, the half-life of U-235, and the multiplication. The lab asks you to use Figure 8.14.

Each square is a share of the original U-235 atoms. Drag the slider to see how much of a half-life it takes for the daughter product to reach about 1%.

Step 1. Find 98.9% parent in the table in Figure 8.14C. How many half-lives have elapsed? Enter the decimal value.

Step 2. Multiply by the half-life of U-235 (listed in Figure 8.14B) to get the age of the sill, in millions of years.

Open Figure 8.14

Table B lists the half-life of each isotope. Table C lists the half-lives elapsed for each percent of parent and daughter remaining. Find the row with 98.9 and 1.1.

Order the geologic events

    8.5C · Reflect & Discuss

    Reflect

    Lab question: Write a question that you have about the geologic history of this location. What geologic evidence would you need to answer the question?

    On your lab page · page 228, 8.5C Reflect & DiscussWrite your question, then the geologic evidence you would need to answer it.

    Answers vary. If you need a starting point, try one of these.

    • When did the fault last move, and what evidence on the fault wall could show it?
    • How long did it take for the sill to cool, and how does that affect the zircon age?
    • What did the area look like when the Fagopsis leaves were deposited?
